1:1: Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
1:2: Habakkuk is using the question form to express his frustration and lament to the Lord.
1:3: Habakkuk is using the question form to express his protest against what the Lord is allowing to happen.
The terms destruction and violence mean similar things. Habakkuk is using the two terms together for emphasis.
1:4: עַל־כֵּן תָּפוּג תּוֹרָה וְלֹא־יֵצֵא לָנֶצַח מִשְׁפָּט

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional.
Habakkuk is speaking of the law as if it were a person who could become physically weak.
Habakkuk is speaking of justice as if it were a person who could go out and act.
1:5: The phrase working a work uses the same Hebrew root for both the verb and its object. This emphasizes the greatness or significance of the action.
1:6: The expression behold me was a common way of introducing a divine announcement.
The Lord is speaking of the Chaldean nation as if it were a person with the emotional qualities of being bitter and hasty.
1:8: The Lord is comparing the Chaldean attack to an eagle rushing to devour its prey.
1:9: The phrase The direction of their faces {is} eastward is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, is only one of several possibilities suggested by scholars.
Here, faces represents the determined direction of the Chaldean advance.
The Lord says that the Chaldean gathers captives like the sand as an extreme statement to emphasize the vast number of people captured.
1:10: The author is speaking of rulers as if they were merely objects of his laughter.
1:11: The Lord is comparing the Chaldean’s advance to the wind to describe how quickly and unstoppably he passes through.
The author is speaking of military might as if it were a god that the Chaldean worships.
1:12: הֲלוֹא אַתָּה מִקֶּדֶם יְהוָה אֱלֹהַי קְדֹשִׁי
Habakkuk is using the question form to affirm that the Lord has existed from ancient times.
The terms The Lord my God and my Holy One mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Habakkuk is speaking of the Lord as if he were a Rock, to emphasize his stability and reliability.
1:13: Here, Your eyes represents the Lord’s ability to perceive and attend to things.
לָמָּה תַבִּיט בּוֹגְדִים תַּחֲרִישׁ בְּבַלַּע רָשָׁע צַדִּיק מִמֶּנּוּ
Habakkuk is using the question form to express his protest against the Lord’s apparent tolerance of treachery.
1:14: Habakkuk is comparing helpless humans to the fish of the sea, which can be caught without resistance.
Habakkuk is comparing humans to a creeping thing that has no one to protect or lead it.
1:15: Habakkuk is speaking of the Chaldean conquest as if the Chaldean were a fisherman pulling people up with a hook.
Habakkuk is speaking of the Chaldean conquest as if the Chaldean were a fisherman catching people with his net and his dragnet.
1:16: Habakkuk speaks of the Chaldean worshiping his net and dragnet as if those things were gods which could receive sacrifices and incense.
Habakkuk is speaking of the Chaldean’s plunder as if it were fat and rich food.
1:17: Habakkuk is using the question form to challenge the Lord about whether the Chaldean will continue conquering without mercy.
2:1: Habakkuk is speaking of his act of waiting for God’s reply as if he were a guard standing at a watchtower.
2:2: Here, run represents the urgent heralding response of the one who reads the message.
2:3: The Lord is speaking of the vision as if it were a living thing that could speak about the end, lie, tarry, and delay.
2:4: The author is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
Here the author is speaking of a proud person as if his soul were something that could be physically puffed up or inflated.
Here, soul represents the entire person from the perspective of his inner character.
Here the author is speaking of moral character as if it were something that could be physically upright or straight.
2:5: The point of this comparison is that just as Sheol is never full and always takes in more of the dead, so the arrogant warrior is never content and always desires more conquests.
The Lord is speaking of wine as if it were a person capable of betraying or deceiving someone.
The point of this comparison is that just as death is relentless and never stops taking people, so this person is relentless and never satisfied in his greed.
2:6: The Lord is using the question form to emphasize that the conquered peoples will certainly mock the oppressor.
הוֹי הַמַּרְבֶּה לֹּא־לוֹ עַד־מָתַי וּמַכְבִּיד עָלָיו עַבְטִיט
Here the conquered peoples use a proverb in order to mock the greedy conqueror.
The conquered peoples are interjecting this brief question form to express frustration that the oppressor’s greed has continued for too long.
2:7: הֲלוֹא פֶתַע יָקוּמוּ נֹשְׁכֶיךָ וְיִקְצוּ מְזַעְזְעֶיךָ
The author is using the question form to emphasize that those who oppose the oppressor will certainly rebel.
The Hebrew word translated biters could mean: (1) your creditors, that is, the plundered peoples who will demand repayment as if they were animals that bite.
Here the author is speaking of those who will demand payment as if they were people who were shaking someone.
Here the author is speaking of the oppressor as if he were plunder that could be taken as spoils of war.
2:8: Here, bloodshed represents the act of murdering people.
2:9: Here the author is speaking of the oppressor building his house in a secure, elevated place as if he were a bird setting his nest on high.
Here, hand represents the power or control of evil.
2:10: Habakkuk is speaking of destroying nations as if it were cutting them off.
2:11: אֶבֶן מִקִּיר תִּזְעָק וְכָפִיס מֵעֵץ יַעֲנֶנָּה
The author is speaking of a stone and a beam as if they were living things that could cry out and answer.
2:13: The author is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
The author is using the question form to emphasize that this is certainly true.
Here the author is speaking as if the results of people’s work were fuel that would be consumed by fire.
2:14: The point of this comparison is that just as the waters completely cover over the sea, so the knowledge of the Lord’s glory will completely fill the earth.
2:15: מַשְׁקֵה רֵעֵהוּ מְסַפֵּחַ חֲמָתְךָ וְאַף שַׁכֵּר
Here the author is speaking of exploiting and humiliating other nations as if it were causing them to drink and making them drunk.
2:16: The word Drink here is a metaphor. The author is speaking of experiencing God’s judgment as if it were drinking from a cup.
Here the author is speaking of being exposed and shamed as if it were being uncircumcised.
Here the author is speaking of God’s judgment as if it were a cup of wine being passed around for the oppressor to drink.
Here, the right hand represents the power of The Lord.
2:17: Here the author is speaking of violence returning upon the oppressor as if it were a garment that would cover him.
2:18: מָה־הוֹעִיל פֶּסֶל כִּי פְסָלוֹ יֹצְרוֹ מַסֵּכָה וּמוֹרֶה שָּׁקֶר
Habakkuk is using the question form to emphasize that a carved image has no value at all.
The author is speaking of an idol as if it were a living person who could teach lies.
Habakkuk is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
2:19: אֹמֵר לָעֵץ הָקִיצָה עוּרִי לְאֶבֶן דּוּמָם
The author is speaking of wood and stone as if they were living things that could wake up and arise.
The author actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. It teaches is said about an idol that cannot speak, making the statement ironic.
The author is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
2:20: Here, all the earth represents all the people living on the earth.
Here, his face represents the presence of the Lord.
3:1: The word shigyonoth is from the original language. Either approach has broad support. The meaning of the word is uncertain, but it may refer to a type of passionate or emotional song.
3:2: Here, your report represents the mighty deeds that people have reported about the Lord.
3:3: The word Teman is the name of a region in Edom, south of Israel.
The term Mount Paran is the name of a mountainous region south of Edom, possibly the southern portion of the Sinai Peninsula.
Habakkuk is speaking of God’s splendor as if it were a blanket that could cover the heavens.
Habakkuk is speaking of God’s praise as if the earth were a vessel that his praise could fill.
3:4: The point of this comparison is that just as the light is intensely radiant, so was God’s brightness.
Here, his hand represents his power or his side.
3:5: Here, face represents the presence of God.
The author is speaking of plague as if it were a living thing that could walk.
The author is speaking of fiery bolts as if they were a living thing that could go out.

The word translated as fiery bolts can refer to different things. This could mean: (1) a burning fever or disease; or (2) flaming projectiles or burning coals, describing God’s destructive power against his enemies; or (3) lightning bolts.
3:6: The word translated as measured is understood in two different ways by Bible scholars. This could mean: (1) God measured out the earth, surveying its full extent; or (2) God shook the earth.
The author is speaking of God’s goings as if God’s ways of acting were physical journeys.
3:7: The author is using the tents of Cushan to represent the people who live in them.
The word Cushan is the name of a people group or region. It may be related to Cush (Ethiopia).
The author is using the curtains of the land of Midian to represent the people who live in the tents.
The word Midian is the name of a place in southern Saudi Arabia. That name came from Midian, a son of Abraham born to Katurah.
3:8: The author is using this question as a way of emphasizing that the Lord’s anger was not truly directed at the rivers.
The author is speaking of the Lord as if he were a fire that burned. This image represents God’s anger.
The author is using this question as a way of restating the previous question for emphasis.
Here, your nose represents the Lord’s anger. The word for nose in the source language is also the word for anger, since a person’s nostrils flare when they are angry.
אִם־בַּיָּם עֶבְרָתֶךָ כִּי תִרְכַּב עַל־סוּסֶיךָ מַרְכְּבֹתֶיךָ יְשׁוּעָה
The author is using this question as a way of restating the previous questions for emphasis.
The author is speaking of God as if he were a warrior who rode on horses and drove chariots. This image represents God coming in power to fight for his people.
3:9: The author is speaking of God as if he were a warrior who readied a bow for battle. This image represents God preparing to act in power against his enemies.
Habakkuk is speaking of Your bow as the means by which the Lord would shoot arrows of lightning.

The meaning of this phrase is uncertain, and Bible scholars have understood it in different ways. Some read it as referring to God acting in fulfillment of the oaths he had sworn to the tribal leaders of Israel. Others understand it to mean that God readied his arrows for battle as he had vowed.
3:10: The author is speaking of the mountains as if they were a person who could see and writhe in pain.
The author is speaking of the deep as if it were a person who could speak. The voice represents the loud sound of the waters.
The author is speaking of the deep waters as if they were a person who could lift hands on high. The raised hands represent the rising waves.
3:11: Habakkuk is speaking of the sun and moon as if they were living things that could have stood still.
לְאוֹר חִצֶּיךָ יְהַלֵּכוּ לְנֹגַהּ בְּרַק חֲנִיתֶךָ
Here Habakkuk is speaking of lightning as if it were arrows and a spear that God uses as weapons.
3:12: Here Habakkuk is speaking of God’s destruction of the nations as if he were a farmer who threshed grain.
3:13: מָחַצְתָּ רֹּאשׁ מִבֵּית רָשָׁע עָרוֹת יְסוֹד עַד־צַוָּאר

Habakkuk is using two images together. He is speaking of the wicked person’s dynasty as if it were a house with a foundation, and he is speaking of God’s destruction of the leader as if it were an execution by beheading, striking the head and laying bare to the neck.
3:14: Here, head represents the leader of the warriors.
Habakkuk is speaking of the enemy warriors’ attack as if they were a violent storm.
Habakkuk is using himself, one person, to represent all of his people.
The point of this comparison is that just as a wild animal devours helpless prey in hiding, so the enemy warriors eagerly attacked the helpless.
3:15: Habakkuk is speaking of God as if God were a warrior riding horses through the sea. He is basing this image on the Israelites’ historic Red Sea crossing. The horses represent God’s power in battle and the sea represents God’s enemies.
3:16: Here Habakkuk is speaking of his inner emotional turmoil as if his belly trembled.
Habakkuk is speaking of Decay as if it were a living thing that could entered into his bones.
Habakkuk is using the day of distress to refer to the occasion when distress would come.
3:17: Habakkuk is speaking of the work of the olive as if it were a person who could be deceptive.
3:19: Here Habakkuk is speaking of The Lord the Lord as if he were strength itself.
The point of this comparison is that just as deer are able to walk with sure footing on steep and rocky terrain, so God gives Habakkuk the same kind of stability and confidence.
Here Habakkuk is speaking of positions of safety and victory as if they were high places on which he could walk.

Here, the chief musician refers to a person who directed the singing and playing of music at the temple. This closing line indicates that the prayer in verses 1–19 was intended for use in temple worship.
Here, my stringed instruments refers to stringed musical instruments used in worship. This indicates how the prayer of verses 1–19 was to be accompanied.
